title: Two sets of cousins
hook: the Pandavas and Kauravas; one palace, two futures

segments.voice: Yesterday: after. Rama crowned, and Hanuman staying as long as the story is told. The story stays.

Cousins who grew up together. Same holidays, same grandparents' house, same photos. Then something breaks between two sides of the family, and now at weddings they sit at opposite ends of the room. The Ramayana was about one family and an enemy outside it. The other great epic, the Mahabharata, is about a family where the enemy is inside. Remember Ganesha breaking his tusk to keep writing? Tradition says this is the book he was writing. This week, just the cliffhangers; the full reading comes later on the path.
screen: `COUSINS AT OPPOSITE ENDS.` → `THE ENEMY IS INSIDE.` → `THE BOOK GANESHA WROTE DOWN.`

segments.voice: Two brothers. The elder, Dhritarashtra, was born blind, so by the rules of the time he was passed over for the throne. The younger, Pandu, became king. Pandu has five sons, the Pandavas. Yudhishthira, the eldest, so honest it becomes a problem. Bhima, huge, hungry and strong. Arjuna, the archer. And the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva. Dhritarashtra and his wife Gandhari, who bound her own eyes with a cloth for life so she'd never see more than her husband, have a hundred sons, the Kauravas. The eldest is Duryodhana. Then Pandu dies young, and his five boys come to live in the palace at Hastinapura with their hundred cousins. One house, the same teachers, the same tables. It goes bad early. Bhima, in play, keeps pinning the cousins, dunking them in rivers, shaking them out of trees. Duryodhana's jealousy becomes hatred. He poisons Bhima and throws him into a river; Bhima survives. When people start calling Yudhishthira the heir, Duryodhana talks his father into sending the Pandavas away, to a house built of lac and other things that burn, meant to be set alight with them inside. Warned in time, they dig a tunnel, set the fire themselves, and slip away. Whose throne is it? Duryodhana is the son of the elder brother, now on the throne. Yudhishthira is the eldest son of the king who reigned. Both have a case. Neither lets go. The poem claims that whatever is here may be found elsewhere, and what isn't here is found nowhere. It starts with two sets of cousins and one house.
screen: `THE BLIND ELDER, THE YOUNGER KING.` · `FIVE PANDAVAS, A HUNDRED KAURAVAS.` · `POISON, AND A HOUSE BUILT TO BURN.` · `WHOSE THRONE IS IT?`

segments.voice: Think of a split in your own family, or a family you know well, two sides that used to share a table, and without picking a winner, picture both at their best: the cousin who made you laugh as a kid, the aunt who drove everyone home. Notice what the split costs everyone. If it feels right, think of one small thing that might someday let two people sit at the same table again.
Pandava, son of Pandu: the name for the five brothers, growing up under one roof with their hundred Kaurava cousins and one throne between them.
Your line: one house. Both sides grew up under the same roof. Day seventy-one, done.

howItsDone: Hindus know the Mahabharata through family retellings, comic books, television serials and temple recitations; tradition names the sage Vyasa as its author and Ganesha as the scribe who wrote it down.

chat.meaning: The Pandavas and the hundred Kauravas grew up in one house. Duryodhana and Yudhishthira each had a claim to the throne, and neither let go.

notes: The Pandavas' divine fathers (Kunti's and Madri's mantra) are left out today for simplicity; a Keeper may want them named.
The epic's self-description ('what is here may be found elsewhere; what is not here is nowhere') is paraphrased; commonly cited as Adi Parva 56.33 (and Svargarohana Parva). Confirm.
Ganesha as scribe is in the vulgate Adi Parva but absent from the critical edition's main text; the script says 'this is the book he was writing' as tradition. Confirm.
Ganguli (1883–1896) is public domain but not on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted.
